> I don't know why you needed a paragraph to say that 1000% memory inflation is a trade-off to optimize dev costs Because that's not what I said. My point was more that a "1000% memory inflation" is not a meaningful cost metric to begin with (to use just one toy example, perhaps you'd agree that going from 10% RAM to 100% has a very different impact than going from 1% to 10%, even though both are a "1000% inflation"). Memory (at least on a personal computer) is not rented by the hour on a per-MB basis; you buy it in bulk. What matters isn't how much memory you could have used but what you'd use the "saved" memory for. Also, when you buy a resource like RAM or CPU as a package, nominal values matter less than under what conditions one of these would reach 100% and my experience may be degraded. For example, if you have 16GB of RAM and you only ever run one program at a time, it doesn't matter to you at all if it uses 3GB or 3MB: you've paid for 16 and the total savings of the 3MB app are zero and in this hypothetical case, there's no tradeoff at all. Now, the average user on the average hardware doesn't use only one GUI app at a time, but they're also not using 200. The only relevant question pertaining to waste is what is the value of 3% memory to your users (integrated over all of them)? In many situations (again, not all), the answer is not much. (And BTW, some developers seem to care about 3% memory more than they do about 3% CPU, even though CPU is much more expensive). When it comes to agent harnesses, the analysis is clearer. On the one hand, people using coding agents are more likely than others to put even a little extra free RAM to some good use, but on the other hand, the cost of using the models themselves is so high that it makes the cost of RAM for the GUI negligible. Saying that a number going up by 1000% is bad is not good engineering. Good engineering requires thinking about the actual value and cost of that number. It varies over time, over app type, over different types of users, and over different kinds of deployments (i.e. how RAM is packaged and paid for).

It’s interesting that Boris Tadić, the former president of Serbia (part of the previous regime, who lost to Vučić 14 years ago) echoes the same type of pronouncements about politicians and the commenters here on HN, and I do not mean this in a particularly laudatory sense. Just recently he was sending messages about how political experience, political vision and the like are key. How to be a political leader one needs this or that, or how Serbia requires this or that type of engagement with future technologies to remain relevant, comparing the student movement to blockchain (yes, really). This (incredibly vain and pompous) man doubtlessly has the most political experience in Serbia right now, and sits in several boards of Chinese and other multinationals, with other consulting roles, pretty much proving the bankability of his political talents. And yet that’s the person behind a series of political decisions and circumstances which inaugurated the previous regime. Also, looking around the globe at professional politicians once also lauded for their political talent, like Macron, or Merkel, I’m really not seeing their policies paying off in spades, nor their "political vision" proving particularly beneficial to their citizenry at the moment. In all three cases, it seems, seasoned politicians made capital errors in judgement which are now causing resentment, almost unprecedented political realignments and upheaval across these nations. People are incredibly quick to judge the potential behaviour of a future political formation - yet Western democracies are by and large falling apart, as a result of career politicians’ actions, inactions, stupidity and avarice? As people speak more and more loudly on certain issues, like Palestine, these same politicians are comfortable ignoring them. Where is the scepticism for them, or the viability of this guild-like way of structuring the political sphere as the way forward? We are living the consequences of having career politicians lead, do we like it so much we cannot conceive of anything better? Anyway, if you look into the local press in Serbia and especially enclaves like Twitter, there’s a wonderful symmetry: the EU champions are terrified the student movement has already shown "concerning" right leanings, they’re busy counting how many EU flags the students have draped themselves in while marching, and aren’t happy. The right is deeply worried about how the "globalist, NGO, pro-EU camarilla" is already deeply embedded in the student movement (they went to Brussels, after all!) and is perhaps even planting their candidates into the mix to sell out the country’s interests to the globalists. I am being slightly ironic here, but I have nothing but contempt for this thinking on both sides. Winning the election required the participation and support from both these camps’ voting blocks, which tells you how bad the situation truly was, since sworn enemies were forced to cooperate with a political unknown just for the chance to win against the existing political regime. In a sense, only a political unknown could have won, as all pre-existing political factions, (mostly comprised of these praised seasoned politicians, many of them three decades into their careers) would not or could not muster the strength or wherewithal to work with one another. No nationalist would ever cooperate with a globalist pro-EU green party, even if it cost them their country, democracy, and those same national interests they hold sacrosanct. Likewise, no progressive citizen party saving democratic principles would ever work with what they view as backward retrograde nationalist movements threatening to plunge the country back into the type of rhetoric and milieu as existed during the wars of the nineties. Also, at some point the decades-long careers of many politicians was perfect cannon fodder for the regime’s propaganda machine, gleefully cataloguing their past sins and outright inventing them if the need arose. After a while, political experience morphs into evidence of one’s political parasitism. It took a decentralised student movement which could not be targeted and besmirched, to engage the non-voting public and voters on both sides of the political spectrum. Part of the reason why all parties which took part in this election were swept away (except for the students and the outgoing regime) was because of failing to recognise the political moment. This election, in my view, was a single-issue election - the workings of democracy and stopping corruption and the further decay of institutions. This is what the political movement will be judged on, and what will determine its political future. The citizenry, at this juncture, is willing to table discussions on foreign policy for the sake of internal affairs and weeding out corruption. Most foreign powers and press corps, sadly, are interested primarily in the foreign policy implications of this new movement, and seem like they couldn’t care less if Serbian citizenry lives in caves, favelas, or in a thriving democracy. Many things are still unclear, such as the exact relationship between the Parliament and Government, once formed, and the direct democracy practiced by the student movement. It is unclear how effective it will prove, or how they will select their allies and collaborators, as it’s perfectly obvious that the movement cannot simply replace the totality of public administration. Regardless, the new regime will enjoy a broad latitude and a measure of good will among the citizenry not seen in a generation. It needs to use that to good effect. If it fails to deliver, they will be ridiculed and attacked by members of both internal factions, and will more than likely splinter, and usher in a return of Vučić, who - lest we forget - is now the only opposition party in Parliament, with a sizeable number of representatives, and plenty of corrosive residuals and slush funds and media operations still at his disposal. Lest we also forget, with 700k party members, it is a powerful organisation even without the corruptive backend of the state apparatus.

It's an incredibly messy space and the particulars are going to vary wildly based on the company. A company in a more regulated space may have the finances to standardize on Siemens or something similarly fancy, but smaller manufacturers may not have any standard at all and you'll be looking at a mix of Rockwell, Allen-Bradley, Honeywell and even more niche brands and PLCs. Many vendors have "proprietary" languages, but they're all going to be very basic stuff that is essentially Visual Basic, C, or JavaScript-ish. It's not going to be a formal software development environment like you're used to. In less regulated environments, a lot of the time you'll find that the PLC/automation component is being handled by the MAINTENANCE or FACILITIES people. So for an example of a problem I'm facing, we have some Vacuum Furnaces. Essentially before you can turn titanium into a useful implant, you have to bake titanium at a temperature above its ignition point so that the molecules can loosen up enough and release the stresses that accumulate in the forging process. As part of this process, there's eight thermocouples of different sensitivities and at least three pressure/vacuum sensors all physically wired into a "chart recorder". The thermocouple "data" is literally a voltage reading, and the chart recorder is interpreting that and converting it into an integer and storing that in RAM. These devices are about 20 years old, and it can only hold about 24 hours of data, so you have to network it with a server that can store those readings in case you ever need to prove to someone that this step of your process was done right. It's not technically complex, but these devices aren't easy to interact with and often require physically connecting to them to make changes. There's all sorts of possibilities for really meaningful integrations with other manufacturing systems, ERP systems, data analysis and visualization, and basically a million "low hanging fruit" problems in the space that simply don't get done because don't have enough people with any technical skill at all. Most companies I've worked for literally don't care about what the solution is, so you get a ton of leeway on architecting the solution. IMO, the best part is that it feels like you're accomplishing something. Making a real impact. You can walk the floor and see the code you wrote building things. Doing things. You know the engineer who came to you with a problem, and you delivered a solution that makes his life easier. Not to make some abstract number go up for a quarterly report, but to actually make things that are useful.

While learning and applying formal verification in the context of using AI agents, what I feel is that sometimes it's hard to express my own thoughts as formal verification. But more than that, I doubt whether formal verification being done correctly actually solves the phenomenon of AI spinning in circles on a specific task. For example, I want to eat chicken, so I try formally verifying "chicken dish," and every time GPT or Claude starts digging into the origin of the sauce in the chicken dish or the breed of the chicken. Then the chicken dish never gets finished and never makes it to dinner, and instead I gain deep knowledge about the origin of chickens. Of course, I know that formal verification has liveness — meaning that there must be progress in the work is also part of formal verification — but the AI judges that learning the origin of the chicken counts as progress too. Yet it ends up doing work that it actually shouldn't be doing. Personally, while organizing these AI anti-patterns, I feel that when you formally verify one condition, verification of another condition gets weakened, and within that phenomenon I sense the AI spinning in circles again. In the end, I end up going through the process of reading and merging everything one by one myself, and I want to know whether this is something only I experience.

I write a spec by speaking, not much thought given to grammar and sentence structure.  I over-describe concepts, over-describe functionality.  A lot of repetition of details and concepts.  The audience is not a human.  Whisper converts it to text. Lightly manually edit for speech rec failures. LLM takes that and converts it into a much much denser, much more structured technical spec in markdown.  This is issue 1 in the repo. I edit this directly extensively, adding detail, removing misconceptions, adding sections with more dictated text. LLM takes this and further densifies it, closer to an actual implementor’s spec.  I carefully note what got added, removed, edited in this step. I edit this carefully and extensively again. Some removals get added back, some additions get removed.  This is the first commit and closes issue 1. I then have an LLM write an implementation plan and basic project scaffolding.  Makefiles, smoke tests, logging, test framework, DI. I edit the plan, and the plan is the second commit.  An LLM uses both plus scaffolding plus my repo policy documents (global) to write a README.  We’re still single threaded. An agent files the first n top level implementation tickets.  These refer to and sometimes quote any interface contracts in the spec or implementation plan.  These usually map 1-to-1 to a module/directory.  These sometimes have stub commits to create the module directory and commit interface definitions.  Some larger modules have a README in their module directory if their purpose or structure or inputs or outputs are complicated or non-obvious. Parallel agents write commit level issues that are the task items for each top level implementation ticket.  One agent per module. Then, spawn parallel agents with detailed global instructions, the full spec+plan, and the full readme, and the full code from the module it is working in, plus the issue text.  Its output is a single commit on the feature branch and a PR that closes out one feature ticket. This spawns an adversarial reviewer which has detailed agent instructions as well as our code style guides and repo policies.  The scaffolding includes tests and linting and checks. Any failures spawn rework agents until the feature branch is up to snuff. I review the feature branch diff and merge it, having read the review and rework comments on the PR.  I frequently add comments about the implementation (“don’t do x, do y”) and add WIP: back to loop it back for more rework.  I don’t see anything that isn’t green, formatted, passes linting, passes tests, and a (dumb) bot thinks is ready to land.  Most of the time, it is.  Sometimes, it did it the wrong way and I correct it. The more modular the code, the easier it is to parallelize (obviously).  It is ridiculously easy to build large software quickly now, provided it is sufficiently modular so the implementation doesn’t have to cross modules very much.  The detailed spec and implementation plan up front helps a lot with this.  It’s a lot like writing multithreaded programs really. Any bugs discovered are tackled with strict TDD, one commit with a failing test, one bugfix commit that must be green and not touch the test. Individual modules must conform to good contracts, meet best OOP practices, and fit into context.  Too big and they get broken down further.  Context size is actually a useful constraint for code structure here. This workflow, the code standards, the styleguide, the linter settings, the fmt settings (obviously only applicable to non-Go as the Go fmt is not configurable), everything is global and stored in another repo and is vendored into each AI managed project repo.  It has a fair bit of “I shouldn’t have to say this, but…” stuff (in the style of “fire codes are written in blood” - each warning sign came from experience). My results are quite good.  It’s as the saying goes, much like managing a team of junior devs.  It is easy to end up with a LOT of parallel implementors, reviewers, reworkers, and tons of CI, but it’s still so much vastly cheaper than humans that it doesn’t matter. Someone will make a LOT of money wringing out the inefficiencies from this workflow, because I think the “agent as replacement for third-world contracted junior dev” model is the one almost everyone is using right now.

For the most part, AI-related biotechs are largely focussing on accelerating the discovery of good candidates. But that's a tiny fraction of the pipeline, which includes lots of lab work (which  can  be automated) and clinical trials (which OTOH require actual human guinea pigs and years of observation and assessment). That is, we can't even model well "how a human body works", much less "how those mechanisms go wrong in each type of cancer". But even if you  could  do all that, for the cures you'd need to figure out what novel, unusual, out-of-distribution thing (relative to your human model) you can throw into the system to avoid the bad behavior, that doesn't kill the person or interfere with other systems or get degraded too quickly or ... tons of other stuff. Highly non-trivial. Maybe lower-hanging fruit is with a novel peptide or antibody, since those are better modeled with ML. Well yeah, cisplatin is used for chemotherapy, but the body of knowledge needed to assess platinum-based drugs in a human body just doesn't exist, and ML isn't gonna intuit it from known data, nor "learn it" since that would require going down to QM, and then integrating that into its model of all human peptides and pathways.) If you have an endpoint with interesting information and you don't want it spammed with requests, require a proof of work from the client, scale up the hardness of it as the load goes up so it never exceeds what's comfortable for you. Even a hard proof of work won't slow down somebody that makes one request per second because they are reading the site but will sighificantly interfere with crawlers that hit you 10000 a second currently at very little cost to them. The module doing proof of work might be a part of your frontend that is static and on CDN. If you want agents still have access to your data, just not through scraping, provide alternative format for them. Like periodic sqlite dump. I made a prototype of such PoW two years ago. A challenge is a random number. Checking the client's solution is calculating one hash of the challenge glued to client's solution and checking if the resulting hash is less than a specific value. The lower the value, the harder the task for the client to do. Client needs to calculate this hash multiple times to find a response that will result (when glued with challenge) with low enough hash. The server needs to keep short lived cache with challenges so the client can't just make up one or reuse another solution and provide two responses for every challenge, first, very small and fast with a challenge, and the second one with actual content (if response was correct). Nothing much worse than CORS preflight.

Instant gratification on rails, essentially. On one hand you have slots/roulette/craps gambling where payout or loss is immediate.  Next come candy crush style games where time invested per session is minimal but extant, but reward continues to stream with flashy graphics for accomplishing subgoals.  Next come longer-term games like 4x or tower defence where there's progression or some sort (often available to skill or how much time you have to spend) where payoff is delayed to the end but there are still progress rewards like new technology or beating a wave of enemies.  Finally RPGs and MMOs where there is (often) no final payout but leveling up, completing quests, acquiring special items, etc. happens at a pace that rewards time spent.  At no time is the next step mysterious; there's a journal with next steps which will each provide their own rewards. Contrast that with real life where reward is on a fixed schedule (N paychecks a month) with no short-term feedback on performance.  At best a short "good work" reward fairly rarely from management.  There are subtler rewards people get like socialization or status, but they aren't on a quest journal and they arrive less frequently for most people. I think for extroverts in high social contact jobs it may actually be as rewarding as gaming, e.g. direct sales. Contractors and spot workers (day laborers, etc.) also get a bit more frequent reward feedback, but far fewer rails unless it's a very canned pipeline of clients. Contrast with the ancestral environment where hunting or gathering had minutes or hours between reward feedback and our natural senses and instincts provided a lot of the rails (hunger, visual attention to animals and edible plants, potential mates).

The reality of what is actually sitting between you and your agents: - A herdr-core background daemon handling JSON-RPC IPC messages. - A crates/ghostty-sys Rust FFI layer binding against libghostty-vt. - A hardware-accelerated GPU rendering pipeline drawing terminal cell glyphs. - A legacy Unix PTY subsystem providing master/slave pairs and terminal line discipline. - An ancient mountain of VT100/ANSI escape codes and termios settings, with resize requests traveling through IPC and SIGWINCH signals notifying Unix terminal applications. - A structured agent-status protocol carried by yet another terminal escape sequence, OSC 7501, then exposed through JSON-RPC. "Nothing" says unfiltered, raw human intimacy quite like reading output from a pseudo-terminal file descriptor and watching \x1b[31m error logs cascade through an SSH pipeline and "pseudo" TTY device drivers. Wrapping this tech in branding that sounds like a sultry, pseudo-erotic pitch is peak HBO Silicon Valley. TTY literally stands for teletype. We are supposedly building the frontier of autonomous artificial intelligence, yet our cutting-edge orchestration layer still routes interaction through abstractions inherited from noisy, electromechanical printing telegraphs of the 1960s. It's not a "native home for your displaced AI souls" -- it's an over-engineered wrapper shackled to the physical heritage of paper rolls and mechanical carriage-return timing: 110-baud Teletypes, separate carriage-return and line-feed operations, and terminal null padding conventions devised to give machinery time to move before the next character printed.  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletype_Model_33

There are apparently 3(?) different technologies in Element alone, depending on which version of Element (desktop, web, mobile). The "old" one is jitsi. The new p2p one appears to be only available to clients that aren't Element? Or you can only create conference rooms in those other clients (commet?), but you can join them from any client. But then those new rooms are sometimes not join-able from Element clients. They just don't appear in the room list at all. Even clicking a link to the room says it's the wrong "room version", but it's a freshly-created room. So I delete the room and make another new one. But now it's a Jitsi room and it doesn't work in this other Element client (all first-party actual Element clients, and all broken in slightly different ways!). So... it's working now, but only after lots of trial and error and lots of cussing from my business partner. And I have to somehow justify that this is better than using Slack/Discord/whatever corporate thing. 3. The official client is fragmented. On mobile, there is Element (classic) and ElementX. You're _supposed_ to use ElementX, since it's the new one, but ElementX does not have all the features of Element (classic), so you might need the Element (classic) client for those things. But Element (classic) is not getting updated, so you're left in the cold as far as updates and the new features (meaning you might not even be able to cross-verify your clients, or join video calls, spaces, etc.) 4. The official matrix server (synapse) is pretty slow. I hosted a couple small communities (~100 people or so?), and synapse somehow kept getting overloaded and crashing. Maybe it needed more than 4GiB, but that seems kind of silly. There are decent 3rd-party clients (continuwuity is my current favorite), but there's no migration path from one server to another without wiping your entire database and starting fresh. So.... my main homeserver is kind of stuck on synapse. 5. Bridges. Yes, you can bridge anything to anything, but have you actually tried it? Interface is super clunky. You have to run a separate bridge service, make sure it swaps keys with the matrix server via a yaml configuration dance, then talk to the bridge's bot in a dedicated matrix channel with special commands that may or may not get your bridge working. I've used signal, discord, telegram, and irc bridges, and they're all a mess in one way or another. My most recent attempt was with the signal bridge. I made the mistake of enabling end-to-end encryption. One day, the bridge server restarted and lost all its encryption keys. Cool, now all the bridged rooms are dead. So naturally, I delete the bridge service and re-configure it from scratch. Now it doesn't work because its bridge bot username was already taken by the previous instance with the lost encryption keys. And I can't just delete that bridge bot user because _matrix does not allow deleting users ever!_. So now I have broken signal bridge rooms and broken signal bot users that I can't ever delete, even with the admin panel. So naturally I open up a postgresql client and delete them manually. Oops, now my matrix database is broken in ways I cannot even begin to comprehend. Because deleting users is not allowed. So now I just can't have a signal bridge. _maybe_ there's a way to make it work, but I've been programming and sys-admin'ing for over 20 years, and it's just beyond me. I'm going to have to (again!) wipe out my homeserver and start over, losing all my messages and contacts (again!). XMPP had very nice transport services, and Psi+ had a very nice UI for configuring and organizing them. 6. Multi-identity support is lacking in all the official and most community clients. If I have a work account and a personal account, I need to start two separate Element clients. Each one is a hefty electron app, and they all have the same systray icon, so I need to trial+error every time to open the right one to message someone. So far, there's only one client I tried that had proper multi-account, and I think it was commet. It was ok, but I hated that it was a flutter desktop app where every click felt super unresponsive. I'm not going to use my work identity for personal chat, just like I'm not going to use my hackernews account to message co-workers. 7. No message auto-deletion. Many people like to claim that Element is more secure than Signal. It is not. If you live in an oppressive country where things you say can easily result in prison or torture, you need more than E2E encryption. You need messages to be gone. pyon is basically correct. --- technical details --- CLRS (3rd edition) defines three types of amortized cost analysis. The first type ("aggregate analysis") requires us to show that for all sequences of  n  operations, the total actual cost of performing those operations in that sequence is less than some function  T(n) . We can then say that the amortized cost of all such operations is  T(n) / n . This makes it necessary that cheap operations precede expensive ones. The second type ("the accounting method") is different: we assign potentially-inaccurate prices to all operations. These prices will be constant regardless of the actual cost of performing those operations. Conceptually, an operation is in "credit" if its actual cost is less than its assigned price, and it is in a state of owing if its actual cost is more than its assigned price. We must then assign prices that make it possible to show that, for all sequences of operations, the total actual cost of all operations from the start of the sequence to point  n  within it is less than the total amortized price assigned by our price schedule. (Stated another way, while an individual operation is free to "owe", a sequence of operations may never be in an "owing" state.) If we can prove that, we are justified in making a claim about the amortized cost of the operations we considered. (Under this method, the amortized cost of an operation is equal to the price we assigned it.) This also makes it necessary that cheap operations precede expensive ones. The third type ("the potential method") defines a potential function which evaluates the state of the data structures maintained by the algorithm. ("Potential" in the sense of potential energy, which can be stored and later released.) It then says that the amortized cost of an operation is equal to the actual cost, plus the difference in "potential state" caused by the operation. Conceptually, if potential is raised, the amortized cost was higher than the actual cost (and has built up a buffer that later operations may draw down), and if it is lowered, the amortized cost was lower than the actual cost. As before, we must show that no sequence of operations can place the data structure into a state of negative potential. Cheap operations must precede expensive ones. ------ Now, why was pyon telling you you should be ashamed of your post? It's almost certainly these two paragraphs: >> If you read more about big-O, you may see the word “amortized” thrown around. That’s a fancy word for “average,” meaning that individual occurrences don’t all behave exactly the same, but over the long run, averaging over many operations, the behavior has a certain characteristic. >> The analysis we’ve been doing is for the average behavior. Lots of operations can behave much worse in unusual circumstances. Adding a key in a dict and looking up a key are O(1), which is true for typical data. But if you understand the internals of dicts, you can carefully craft a set of keys that will perform terribly, with O(N) behavior. Filling that dict would take O(N²) time. Your post has confused average-case analysis with amortized analysis. (And it makes this problem worse by implying that the two terms refer to the same concept.) The  point  of amortized analysis is that you cannot see worse performance than the amortized cost. An amortized analysis is deterministic and averages runtime costs over the different operations that are present in a sequence of operations beginning from a given initial state; an average-case analysis is stochastic and averages runtime costs of a single operation over many different performances of that operation against different initial states. These two terms are not synonymous and they don't belong to the same universe of terminology; if we're thinking about "average-case analysis", then an amortized analysis is a type of "worst-case analysis", not a type of average-case analysis. The first paragraph I quoted tells us that you're talking about amortized analysis, but you aren't: the example you provide is of an average-case analysis. If the amortized cost of adding a key to a dictionary were O(1), it would be impossible for adding a sequence of N keys to that dictionary to take more than O(N) time. (As is in fact the case for the Python list.append example you mention beforehand.)

You gave your agent access to your system with  your  permissions. Then you asked it to do something that you can do with your permissions, and it did. The correct thing, and this isn't hard, is to give it a different set of permissions than yours. Do not let it get into your .ssh directory at all, problem solved. People keep posting these stories as if there's something useful in them, and there is: The moral of the story is don't be a fool. Give your agents different, restricted, permissions, than your own permissions. This is the same approach when working with people. Your agent should be, from an authentication and authorization perspective, treated like any other employee: Given an appropriate set of permissions to their needs, not root level access to all your systems.

I started thinking about agentic programming from a totally different perspective. Personal accountability in software development is actually hard, and less useful than it seems. What good is it if you discover a 12 y.o. vulnerability and can blame a specific person? (Like the recent one in PHP?) You may learn the name of that programmer who made the mistake, but it does not really tell you anything about that person, unless their overall record is terrible, and you are not entitled to any damages anyway. In closed source, this is even worse. So a certain Windows function sucks. Now what. You never learn any other provenience than "Microsoft did it". Tough luck even getting support, and you certainly don't get your license fee back. This sort of accountability is worse than useless. The only exception I see is knowledge  within  a specific development team. We usually know what sort of errors our colleagues are prone to, and we may be able to work around their personal weak spots. Agentic coding done well has a dimension of trust that human coding cannot achieve. I can tell my agents to aim for 100 per cent test coverage without overburdening them or running out of budget and time. I can ask other agents and other models to review code written by the first agents, and then again. Every layer of such review adds some credibility to the result, and its mechanistic character ensures certain level of repeatability. Sure, it can happen that all involved mechanisms share the same weakness and let a particular bug through. But it is similar to several sieves over one another lining up perfectly to let something through, and that is quite rare. If I had to choose, I would trust code designed, implemented and reviewed by three different SOTA models over code designed, implemented and reviewed by three median programmers today. Three elite programmers would have been a different story, but that would also be expensive like hell, and much like you don't eat most of your dinners in a Michelin restaurant, you have to economize with your code development in a similar way.

I attribute much of Stack Overflow's decline to a mismatch of scaling... and that mismatch is in part what lead to the perceived hostility by askers and answerers.  Overcorrection and changes (frequently removing of curation tools) often made this worse.  (Part of this is inspired by a recent post on meta.stackexchange about how corporate is redoing question deleting and Shog's answer to it  https://meta.stackexchange.com/a/420032  ) The scaling focuses around discoverability, (the rate of) asking questions, and the amount of time available for people to curate (which includes helping new users get onboarded). Much of the early days of Stack Overflow, discoverability was trivial.  It was easy to find an interesting question because few things were asked and this was the days when there was a  lot  of changes.  We're dealing with 2008 and beyond - there were a lot of new frameworks and languages being updated then... Spring 3, Backbone, Knockout, Angular, React, Vue, Spring Boot 1, Java 7 and eventually Java 8. This was a time of rapid change and the experts were answering on Stack Overflow - and it was scaling up to meet that demand with additional tools. But it also started becoming a place where students were posting questions (every September you'd get the "how do you draw a triangle with stars?" questions 20 times a day in the Java or Python tags...) This started being visible in 2010 with question quality and by 2014 it was a full on epidemic. One part of this is that the original community of people who followed Jeff and Joel's blogs and helped barn raise the site had gotten smaller as an overall portion of the site because of that explosive growth.  Some people wanted it to be a place where any user could get help with a question (and closing questions was antithetical to that) and others were looking for it to be more of a wikipedia.  That conflict still simmers. Another part of this is that a smaller and smaller percent of the overall user base was using the curation tools available.  Fewer people were closing questions (that really did need to be closed) and helping onboard new users with expectations.  When there are 6000 new questions a day that represents a  lot  of work for the volunteers to try to onboard them.  Initially, everyone came from the same point and there wasn't much onboarding needed.  With its growth, a lot of new people were coming to it from the approach that it was a forum or immediate feedback chat. That growth without scaling up the tools for onboarding and curation (making it  easier  to do) meant that the people trying to help new users and make discovery of well written questions easier had less time per user (or question) to do so... and got increasingly curt - they couldn't spend 5 minutes per question anymore and instead were trying to do things in 30 seconds or less. This was the beginning of "Stack Overflow is unfriendly." The attempt that corporate had from this, instead of making it easier to help people took away curation tools and close reasons were made more specific... which in turn meant that the people trying to close questions to make discoverability of well written questions on the home page easier were incredibly pedantic in order to meet those reasons. Some of the tooling is set up to be able to handle 6000 questions per day, and scales poorly back to having 100 questions per day. The user base of Stack Overflow at 2 months old is  very  different than Stack Overflow today, even if it has the same question rate.  There are very few people who are around to help onboard users (diamond mods if you read this - there's 25 of you and 100 questions per day... you can spend 5 minutes per new question per day to help onboard the user for expectations and still have half an hour a day for other moderation tasks). Many of the people who did curation when SO was growing and at its peak have become disappointed with Stack Overflow and while they may look at it to see if its a site where their contributions would again be appreciated... though the changes that corporate appears to want have been additional curtailment of curation tools and have even proposed removing close votes all together (  https://meta.stackoverflow.com/questions/438185/the-company-...  ). --- Stack Overflow is mostly dead.  It lingers on, but every change that is being attempted or proposed in trying to get more "engagement" takes it further and further from being a place where new knowledge is collected and collated. I would attribute this mostly to there aren't any curators left - so everything they try building turns into a mess.  Corporate has leaned too hard on the community to do curation and diamond mods have largely stopped doing curation in favor of moderation. With low activity and the largest ratio of staff and diamond mods to active users, this would be an excellent time for those two groups to completely take up the task of curation and onboarding to set a new standard for how it should be done... and if they aren't willing to do it, that really suggests that the final nail in the coffin is in place waiting to get hammered.

On most devices that aren't PCs, there is no separate firmware - the firmware is part of the software. The boot ROM is just loading a sector and jumping to it. You may implement UEFI as your second or third boot stage if you want to, but it's your responsibility. You wouldn't want the boot ROM to implement UEFI. It would have many unpatchable bugs and different ones on every device revision. Better to put the UEFI where you can patch it. For instance on a Pinephone booting from SD card,  the firmware is on the SD card . Moving the SD card to a different device is putting the wrong firmware on that device, that's why it doesn't boot. And then once you're shipping your own UEFI impl and shipping a kernel that runs inside UEFI, as part of the same SD card image, the next obvious step is to wonder why you can't short circuit those two layers and run the kernel directly on the hardware.

There are likely valid points made here, but I think the conclusions are considerably too strongly held. For one thing, it's already clear that humans value the achievements of other humans outside of their pure economic value. We are impressed by the athletic, artistic, and intellectual abilities of other humans, even in fields where we are surpassed by machines or computers. Cars have been faster than humans for a century, but we still value Olympic sprinters. Computers have been superior at chess for decades, but we've all still heard of Magnus Carlsen. AI can now produce art that only the most talented humans could hope to replicate, but most of us aren't particularly interested, because there's no human mind behind it. So assuming we did somehow manage to create a post-scarcity world, I think people would still want to learn and to improve their skills. And we would still value those skills. There would also still be work to do; work that either people do because they want to, and/or that we don't want computers doing for us. Much of it work that in today's world is undervalued. In that utopian world, there would also be room for hobbies that could fill some of the human need to produce value that work currently does. Lots of people would love to be able to learn a craft or play a sport but don't currently have the time, money, or energy to do so. I have plenty of concerns about the impacts of AI on the world, but IF we do somehow manage to get the good outcome where it truly is transformative and the benefits manage to be at least somewhat evenly distributed... well, I agree that we won't all just hang out, but I do think we'd be ok.

> On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences. The weird thing is to see this based off the KV-Cache in the diagrams. Completely different from the Databricks RAFT [1]. My team built "Dreamtime" earlier this year [2], which used a different mechanism to distill out learnings across multiple sessions. This didn't pull from the token layer, but from user nudges on unsatisfactory responses. This works like a sawtooth wave where we accumulate context, check for dissonances (a user gets to say "It depends" and fix it), compress it back, retire the old one. The audit requirements are the real problem for customers, where you need to be able to ask "When did this change? and who changed it?" which was hard to answer from the lowest layer of the model unless you can retain lineage to the original sessions. A model we train can't serve as an accomplice to a user who wants to hide some financial crimes by nudging the agent repeatedly. [1] -  https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10131

Since we last built Flint earlier this year ( https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48834924 ), we have been wondering if interactive charts can also find they home in terms of simple high-level specifications to allow AI agents to produce them easily, reliably and with high-quality. I have always been amazed by NYT interactive stories back in school, as they can always tell a fun story without super long verbose text write-ups; thus I have been wondering what if they can just be as easily created as any basic charts to make them easier to create everywhere.
Despite the AI models now are more capable of creating interactive artifacts, we find creating interactive charts still kinda annoying (esp. if you are building them to serve users directly in their chat, in your data apps). Agents (especially with smaller models) quite often generate interactions with undesired effects, they are often quite slow, costly, and extremely annoying if to want to steer it to change something. Most times, I find that if I ask the agent to change interaction, it can randomly change style, layout, even the data. We find the issue is that the language agents use to create interactive visualization is kinda low-level. The logic for specifying data encoding, style and interactions are all entangled (if you swap x,y axis, you are likely going to redo your interaction and layout again). Thus, despite agents have been working hard, it is essentially doing lots of stuff bottom up. We decide to design a language that can separate the visual logic and the interaction logic to make specification much cleaner, manageable, and friendly (to both human and AI). The magic here is that we are now disentangle the logic at the spec level, but make the compiler to do the heavy lifting (sorry, compiler!) to wire up logics to support easy composition and adaptation of the logics to create a expressive interactive charts. We used a trick of bidirectional transformation to help the compiler maintain the mapping between pixel/visual space to data semantics so the specs can stay at a higher-level. We made a video to explain the ideas.  https://youtu.be/JAJy7ToczMs  Some principles we had in the design: - the language should be high-level and the agents can easily user them in chats/apps declaratively (with many presets). - the language should not give up expressiveness. We also provide a programming API, so that you can use it to create charts in your app/dashboards for external interactions. The expressive API also makes it possible to compose very cool bespoke interactions (the spinning globe in the website). To try it out: - You can try Flint in your agent app. Simply call your agent to create it as an MCP app in your chat! ( https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/#/mcp ) - If you are building applications, ask the agent to use the library. Flint is especially suitable for building agentic apps where you want agents to bring up an interactive charts quickly in the user session following their asks. - Btw, the flint mcp app allows you create interactive dashboard in the chat as well. Finally, I'm thinking that despite AI agents are now so good at coding, that they seem to be able to create EVERYTHING. It might not just be the time to give up designing new languages to make it easy to describe and create stuff. In the end, language is still the way for us to communicate with the computer, I think the alignment of programming language between human and AI in could probably make building, steering easier.

I work at OpenAI and I can try to explain our logic. In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra Even today, I'd recommend this as a general starting point for picking models. If you care about quality only, pick Astra. If you're a bit price sensitive, pick Sol. If you're very price sensitive, pick Terra or Luna. Of course, model size doesn't capture all variation. Models that are trained later might have new data or new techniques or new architectures that earlier models lack. You can see this with models from all providers - Sonnet 5.5 outperforms Fable 5.1 in ways, and Gemini 3.8 Flash outperforms 3.1 Pro in ways. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. If you have suggestions on how to name our products better, I'm all ears. Our intention is to make things clear and simple, even if we miss the mark sometimes. Unfortunately, a lot of the complexity is somewhat irreducible and due to to the actual complexity of the products. Scaling model size is different from scaling reasoning effort which is different from scaling multi-agent count. So if we just swept all of those under a single name of "more IQ", it would make the naming simpler but the experience much worse, as important details would be obfuscated from end users.

I built Doozy because support at my company (Spur) is understaffed and kept waiting on engineering to run a query for a customer, or to check whether something was a bug. The first version was a Slack bot with read access to our Postgres and Stripe, and it was very hacky. It could barely read files sent in a thread, but the agent was smart enough to find them through Slack search and finish the task anyway. It got used far more by support and success than by engineers, which surprised me. 13 people at Spur use it every day; it's basically a critical part of the team now. Doozy is the rebuilt, multi-tenant version. You mention it in a thread with a task, it runs the task against your systems (database, Stripe, GitHub, Linear, PostHog, any MCP server, the web) in its own isolated environment, and posts the result and files in the thread. How it touches production: - Every job runs in a fresh sandbox (E2B today) with no credentials in it. Model calls, tool calls and git go through gateways outside the sandbox that add credentials per request. A prompt injection can make the agent misuse the tools it has, but it can't exfiltrate a key, because there isn't one to read.
- Secrets the agent genuinely needs inside the sandbox (an SSH key, a CLI token) are handed over only when it asks for a named secret with a reason, and that request is logged.
- Tools marked destructive start denied. Owners turn them on per tool.
- Every external action writes a receipt in the thread and an append-only audit log. Per-workspace pricing, no seats. 14-day trial, no card, install takes a couple of minutes. Happy to go deep on the sandbox and gateway design.

It depends on the operating mode you choose and your prompt/AGENTS.md file. The "Act" operating mode has strict guardrails, and a card only moves into review if the agent explicitly asks for your review (via tool call) or has a question. It's less prone to unnecessary interruptions. For example agents often decide to pause during a multi-phase plan even though no human input is needed. If an agent decides to pause in this mode, the harness automatically nudges it forward. The "Explore" operating mode works more like most other harnesses: if the agent decides it's done then it lands in review. Most recent models (pretty much anything released within the past year) will automatically run tests before it thinks it's done, but you can define this for example by specifying a TDD approach in AGENTS.md. In practice when a task is sitting in review, the agent typically provides a summary about test status; and this is without any special guidance. I also implemented a "Plan" operating mode, but nowadays models are good enough at following instructions that it might be a bit overkill. This mode mounts the workspace as read-only. I originally made this out of frustration when I used to use Cline (the agent would make changes even when their plan mode was enabled). Another reason why it's overkill is because each task in MIKE already has an isolated workspace. This mode still has some advantages though, especially if you have independent subtasks that can run in parallel.

In working with local models, the main issues I've seen are failed tool calls, getting stuck in loops, or some other upstream issue with the inference server. Auto-retry logic helps keep things going, and tasks will sit in review for your action if they get stuck. In those situations, you can either adjust the instructions or change to a more... obedient model and put it back in the work queue. I've experimented with a few inference services too, which tend to have other issues like how they handle rate limits. I added configurable client side limits (concurrency and reqs per minute) to make this run more smoothly. For programmatic access: this features a RESTful Web API using a Bearer token for authorization. After generating a token (via Settings -> About), you could them have a cronjob run basic curl with a payload to start tasks. I haven't spent much time on the documentation for this yet; the current docs were generated by agents so they're a bit painful to read. I only reviewed them for accuracy. Thanks for checking it out!

It takes time and effort to find vulnerabilities. GPUs are still a moving target, with frequent new models, and many different chips, with multiple companies producing different PCBs. Game consoles are a more static target by contrast. You would need a juicy target, easy to procure for cheap for the effort to make sense. It's probably doable, though I suspect that more recent models are probably better protected against that sort of attack. These are performance-oriented chips though, not security-oriented, so they probably make a few compromises. They may also use chiplets with a more secure "secure element", I have no idea (though you still need to communicate with it). I don't think I've seen anyone attempt it, so it may be that they haven't specifically hardened their designs against these attacks. Then comes the question of practicality: would you solder a "modchip" to your GPU? It may even be hard to reach the correct spot without interfering with cooling. I would bet that this is doable with the same setup as the RP2350 hack, but that requires drilling into the specific chip that you are targeting, so great, but not very useful: there probably aren't many secrets to extract, you could decrypt the BIOS (I thought these were just signed with asymmetric keys?) and try to find an exploit in the code there, I guess. But this specific technique is not useful for putting your own firmware then using the chip. Anyway, it's probably doable to glitch the power supply of some mid-to-late 2010s nvidia GPUs to have it accept custom BIOSes, though graphics card are specifically designed to keep the power supply stable, so you would have to desolder a lot of capacitors (and reconnect them after startup is finished?).

I used to use DD-WRT, and Tomato, and Shibby's mod of Tomato, and Advanced Tomato, and other stuff.  Somewhere, I'm sure I still have a WRT54GS that I hacked ~20 years ago to accept SD cards.  It was a fun time in using inexpensive hardware in unintended ways. At one point, and I don't remember exactly when, I just started using OpenWRT instead.  It wasn't always the case, but it presents a very usable GUI straight away these days and it has a ton of flexibility for getting creative later. At home I run it on a Pi4 that I bought for the purpose.  It keeps up with my 500/20Mbps DOCSIS internet very well indeed.  I've used it with a USB NIC to get dedicated ports, and also with VLANs and a managed switch instead.  I just download and flash the card, plug stuff in, and configure it.  No real issues -- for years, now.  (Wireless is provided by Mikrotik access points.) When something faster happens in my neighborhood (which may be very soon; I had a very brief chat with a dude whose fiber splicing trailer was parked across the street just yesterday), I'll probably want to move to something more capable. That could be in the form of faster Pi, or an old PC running OPNsense -- or even stick with OpenWRT.  No big deal. If I really wanted a tidier package for light-weight travel or something, then I guess I'd pick something appropriate from glinet and put an official OpenWRT image on it. For heavier-travel, I've got a kit with a Pi4, a managed PoE switch, and a backup Mikrotik box (that can be a switch or a router; it runs OpenWRT as well and the normal config is that it just provides more switch ports), and all this stuff is mounted onto a 1U rack shelf that is in-turn inside of a road case.  It's meant to be physically durable and to include enough gear that if any part of it dies then I can replace that functionality Right Now without spending time finding parts in the middle of nowhere. So, no:  I would not buy one that was prefabulated.  It wouldn't scratch my itch. --- For everyone else?  Honestly, the regular folks I know who ask me questions about networking aren't  into  that stuff at all or they wouldn't be asking.  They don't care about ultimate speeds, or latency under load, or any of those things.  They don't care about running Internet services from their network, or services on their local network, and probably don't even have a printer to abuse if something goes awry.  They're also not interested in exploring the bowels of their home to install cabling for PoE access points. They just want decent-enough wifi coverage that they don't have to think about it, and then:  They want to succeed at not thinking about it. So for those folks, I've come to recommend proprietary multi-node mesh systems.  It doesn't really matter to me which one it is, or how terrible some aspect or other is:  They all tend to check the right boxes, they update themselves, and then:  Nobody thinks about them.
